utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in the courtroom and those who are listening to our trial. If there are no procedural matters, the witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Please sit down. Welcome back to the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have to remind you that the affirmation to tell the truth still applies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And Mr. Tolimir is continuing his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. May peace reign in this house. I wish this day and the whole trial to end in accordance with God's will and not necessarily my will. I will also like to greet the witness and welcome him again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yesterday we were talking about evacuation, so yesterday we were talking about the evacuation and who were aware of that evacuation and who gave their approval. I asked you whether you saw on the 19th of July in Mladic's possession the agreement that was reached for the evacuation of civilians. You said that you were aware of this agreement but that you don't remember exactly whether you saw it there. I would like to show you 7246; that's the 65 ter number. 7247 actually, I apologise. And it also I think has a P number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please give us the P number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, 65 ter document 7247 has not been tendered or admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just so we can start off with a bit of clarity about the various meetings, I don't think I'm mistaken, but the meeting to which General Tolimir is referring wherein General Smith in the report observed that Mladic was carrying agreement was the meeting on the 25th of July at the Jela Restaurant. I think it's clear from the reports that are in evidence that that is the meeting to which we are talking or to which he is referring, just so we can get oriented to time and place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Is that your position, Mr. Tolimir?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not asking about the timing of that meeting. What I want to ask him about is what agreement he saw in General Mladic's hands. And that's why I wanted to take a look at 7247, that's the 65 ter number, so that the General can see what I'm going to ask him about. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is on the screen now. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this is your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 19, paragraph 6, in Serbian. Okay, now we can see it. I'm not sure exactly which page in English that is. I'm going to read what I'm interested in so that we can find it in English. It's page 8 in the English language. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "On the 25th of July, I met General Mladic at Han Kram in order to discuss the situation in Zepa and to follow up on aspects of the agreement I had signed with him on the 19th of July. Mladic was accompanied by General Gvero. The subject of Zepa dominated the meeting. Mladic arrived carrying an agreement signed by Bosnian officials providing for a cease-fire. The evacuation of civilians less men of military age and the arrangements for the exchange of prisoners under UNPROFOR auspices. After a two-hour meeting, I decided to move to Zepa and continue the meeting with Mladic there in order to assess the situation for myself and to assist with the Bosnian agreement on the evacuation of the wounded." My question is, Do you remember now that you stated that Mladic had an agreement signed by Bosnian officials? Can you tell us anything about that agreement? Can you tell us whether you saw it? Did he show it to you? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the details of the agreement. I remember he had it and I -- I expect he showed it to me. But I don't specifically recall its form or substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So you do remember what you stated here in your statement, that the agreement was about the cease-fire, about the evacuation of civilians except the men of military age; is that true? And also it pertained to the agreement about the exchange of prisoners under UNPROFOR auspices. Can you confirm that those elements were present in that agreement?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am saying it when I'm making that statement, then I expect that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that on the 25th when you arrived there, as you said, to help reach and sign the agreement about the evacuation of the wounded, can you then tell us whether they spoke about it with the Muslim side, because you saw this agreement that they signed, the agreement for the evacuation of civilians and everybody else except men of military age?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm clear that this was a result of the two sides talking. Indeed, if not on that day, on another day, I was present when they were both talking, as we've seen in that video.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, can we now have 151. It's -- no, actually, I apologise. D51. Thank you to e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this is the basic agreement signed by the representative of the Zepa authorities. Can you take a look at item number 7. This was signed on the 24th; that's what we can see in the first paragraph, signed on the 24th of July and so on and so forth. And then item 7 goes as follows: "In accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12th of August, 1949, and the additional protocols of 1977, the civilian population of Zepa shall be given the freedom to choose their place of residence while hostilities continue." And I emphasise that: "While hostilities continue." My question is: This probably was in the agreement that he mentioned earlier because this agreement also talks about the evacuation of able-bodied men; so is this the agreement that the Muslim authorities signed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't -- I cannot confirm that that is what they signed at that time at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you now take a look at item 3 where it says that Avdo Palic is supposed to order his soldiers to withdraw. I will repeat. Avdo Palic has to order his soldiers to withdraw from the defence lines together with the population from the centres of inhabited places and villages and not to try to cross illegally through the territory of Republika Srpska. My question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is very complicated. You are not putting the text, the real text, of the document to the witness but you put your interpretation of the -- this agreement, item 3, to the witness, which is quite complicated. And then you want to add a question. This is, I think, not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I was reading this very bad original that we have on the screen, so maybe I inserted a word or two. So I'm going to try to read it again: "Avdo Palic shall issue an order to his troops to withdraw from the defence line and refugee groups together with the population and from the centre of settlements/villages" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. This is item 2. You indicated you wanted to read item 3. Now you are reading item 2; this is a different matter.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Mr. President, I apologise to you and to the witness and to everybody listening. When I said paragraph 3, I meant their sequence from the top of the page. But it is actually numbered as paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Avdo Palic shall issue an order to his troops to withdraw from the defence line and refugee groups together with the population and from the centre of settlements/villages and not to try to cross illegally through the territory of Republika Srpska." This was paragraph 2. My question is: If you look at this item of the agreement, can we conclude that Muslims had the obligation to withdraw and then come to the centre of the village and then from that point evacuation would be carried out? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I can conclude that in that I don't know the provenance of this document. You told me it is the one that was in the hands of Mladic and then you weren't so sure. And secondly, I can see at the bottom of the original -- from the bottom of the original that Palic hasn't signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. I told you first that Mladic had in his hands a document signed by the Muslim functionaries from Sarajevo, while this agreement is an agreement signed by the representative of the Zepa civilian authorities together with General Mladic. Can we now take a look at item 5. I quote: "Avdo Palic shall start disarming his units immediately. And all the weapons" -- now I can't read this bit, "... shall be handed over to the VRS representative in the UNPROFOR base in Zepa." So is this an obligation on the military and Avdo Palic to disarm and surrender their weapons to the VRS in the UNPROFOR base in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't see that that -- I go back to my last point. Palic has not signed this agreement. And as I understand it, he was the commander of the Bosnian armed forces in that enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And just as you, whoever, drafted this document is committing the ICRC, UNPROFOR, UNHCR to carry out certain tasks, nobody invited UNPROFOR and I'm absolutely certain they didn't invite the ICRC to put their signatures to these documents, or this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Is this the first time you see this document here in the courtroom, or were you aware at the time that this document was signed back then in Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this is the first time I have seen this specific document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of which document did your team arrive in Zepa and carry out the evacuation? Which agreement? Which document was it?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall except that it was the one in Mladic's hand on the day -- on the 19th, I think it was, if I get my dates right, that we -- that I came to -- when you've quoted me in my statement. And I can't remember now whether that's the 19th or the 25th. But on that day I had seen him with a document and we then went to Zepa. And I suspect the document was in Serbo-Croat, which I can't read, so I was taking its interpretation for what I was told it said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you do not know this document, although your people took part in the evacuation in accordance with the agreement, I would like us to tell -- I would like you to tell us the following: You said that Avdo Palic didn't sign it; however, were you as a soldier responsible and did you have a duty to carry out the political decisions of the political functionaries of your state and also of the United Nations during your term in Bosnia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've got -- I didn't follow your question properly. And in the record it says an "injury state," and I'm not quite clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We heard the interpretation of "your state."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ah. I was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it's corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. My political authorities and the people I was responsible to politically were the United Nations and my -- and as I've explained to you, there was a parallel chain of command in which the military chain of command worked back to the department of peacekeeping in the United Nations. And while I was required in every way to co-operate, co-ordinate, and so forth with the political direction of the United Nations, my authority as a military commander was to make my decisions and give my orders to my command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We heard your answer which was slightly more expanded than I expected, so maybe we lost the essence of the answer. What I want to know is whether you on one side and Avdo Palic on the other side were duty-bound to carry out the orders given to you by the political authorities of your respective countries? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer for Palic or, for that matter, the Bosnian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you aware of the fact that Hamdija Torlak, the person to whom you spoke, was the representative of the Muslim population and the military in the negotiations with the VRS? He arrived at Boksanica as their representatives. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not clear that he was the representative for military matters in this negotiation, and I don't believe he could speak for them. Not least because we've already seen from the correspondence with the -- with President Izetbegovic that he saw -- he, the president, saw that there was a difference between the authorities of the civil community within Zepa and the military of Bosnia-Herzegovina overall.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. I think this is your opinion. The documents, however, tell a different story.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at D55, page 30. I want to see what Mr. Avdo Palic says about this evacuation. So can we have in e-court page 30, paragraph 108.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And Avdo Palic says the following: "President, at about 21 hours, negotiations in Boksanica, Rogatica, at which General Smith, Torlak Hamdija," the person we just mentioned, "president of Executive Board of Zepa, and war criminal Ratko Mladic were present, concluded. As General Suvalic informed me today during these negotiations, an agreement about the exchange of all for all, accepted also by our side, should have been adopted. Minister Muratovic was supposed to be present at these negotiations but he was not because security was not guaranteed for him. General Suvalic also informed me about this. During the negotiations, General Smith stated that our side did not accept the agreement about the exchange of all for all and that our side was looking for some additional concessions. Hamdija Torlak remained at the place of negotiations in Boksanica, and he was told that if we are prepared to accept the exchange of all for all during the night or until 0800 hours in the morning, General Smith will let us know so that the plan of helicopter evacuation could be prepared. President, I ask you on behalf of my brigade, which is on the verge of nervous breakdown, if our side does not accept the agreement to undertake everything so that it accepts the agreement and free us from torture, we cannot believe that this problem looks like you will not solve it. If this problem is not resolved in the course of tomorrow, I must make a decision tomorrow to make a break-through towards you with 2.000 men and 10.000 rounds, whoever will cross over, and you have the picture of Srebrenica and obtained intelligence data," and so and so forth. Then further below, line 18, he says: "President, I ask you in the name of soldiers who have been fighting for the last 15 days like lions. I ask you in the name of fallen soldiers. And in my ranks I have sons or parents of those who died. I ask you in the name of evacuated families and children who are just waiting to meet their fathers, who are left on Zepa mountain to be slaughtered or annihilated in any other way. I ask you again in the name of my soldiers to make it possible for us to defend Bosnia in some other battle-fields, to liberate it, and to die like people. Do not let us die of hunger, of most common diseases, because we do not have a single doctor, but already have sick people who cannot, if we start the break-through, to get through to the free territory." So this was a long quote. Do you see the position of Avdo Palic here? Was his position that both the population and the military should be evacuated from the non-demilitarised zone of Zepa into the territory controlled by the BiH army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see that that is what he's asking his president to arrange or to make happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does Avdo Palic recognise Torlak as the negotiator on behalf of the army and the population and is he saying that he will wait in Boksanica until you get the consent of the Muslim Presidency? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He says that he is making -- he is negotiating, if I recall. Can we go back to the first page of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Not the first page, the previous page.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The previous page, correct. I'm sorry. He says that Torlak is conducting and has conducted the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does he call him "our negotiator" in this document? Hamdija Torlak is in Boksanica, et cetera. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if he says "our." I can't see "our" there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that Avdo Palic recognizes members of the War Presidency to be negotiators, those who are in charge of the army and civilians who are exercising all authority in war time in the territory of the enclave of Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't mean it as you've stated it. It says that, in that Palic is supposed to have written this or said it, that Torlak is conducting the negotiations. It doesn't say that he is in charge of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does Avdo Palic want the soldiers and civilians to leave the enclave of Zepa, and is that what he says in his letter to Alija Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly he is wanting to get them out, and he would like to get them out by helicopter. If not, he is going to have to walk them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you yesterday whether anyone had obstructed the implementation of the agreement or the evacuation of civilians and soldiers from Zepa and you said that no one did that. Can you please answer that question now. Was anybody obstructing the process or dragging their feet? Because yesterday we read that letter of Alija Izetbegovic saying that it was the Serbs who were taking their time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not entirely clear. I think I answered last time that apart from particular incidents, one of which was reported me involving you, I don't recall the evacuation of the population as being obstructed once we had got the arrangements clear. What we have here is an argument going on about the arrangements.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. I understand what you are trying to say. My question is: Was anybody delaying the evacuation of soldiers from Zepa in accordance with the agreement? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I'm trying to explain to you that we didn't have an agreement at this stage. The -- there is no trust shown in what it is you've put before me whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I put the agreement to you. 1D151.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could that be shown once again, the heading and the first paragraph underneath that. And then could the signatories and signatures be displayed as well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You see where it says "agreement"? That's what it also says in English. And then it says "following the disarming of military-aged men in Zepa," and the signatures are those of Rajko Kusic; Sejmon Dudnjik, commander of UNPROFOR; Ratko Mladic, head of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska; and Hamdija Torlak, a member of the War Presidency of Zepa who negotiated on behalf of the soldiers and inhabitants of Zepa. So do you see the document now? Does it have legal force and the consent of all the protagonists in this event? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: For the record, this is D51. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, for the record, I'd like it to be clear whether or not General Tolimir's question where he describes Hamdija Torlak as negotiating on behalf of the soldiers and inhabitants of Zepa, whether that's something he's pulling out of the agreement or if that's just something he's building into the question. Because up to then I think he was quoting from the agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, could you clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The next document is going to clarify that. This is a document that the witness is familiar with too. P --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, no. You put -- you were going to put a question to the witness. But before you did this you said: "And then it says: 'Following the disarming ..." and so on "... and Hamdija Torlak, a member of the War --" I think it should read, "a member of the War Presidency of Zepa who negotiated on behalf of the soldiers and inhabitants of Zepa." That was your statement before you were going to put a question to the witness. Mr. Thayer asked you to clarify this. Is it your position that he negotiated on behalf of the soldiers, not only of the inhabitants of Zepa? And you were discussing that with the witness quite a long time now. Please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you. Thank you to Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could the witness please tell us whether he knew that not all the inhabitants and soldiers could take part in the negotiations, rather it could only be the representatives of these categories that had requested evacuation from Zepa; did you know that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not everybody could stand there and negotiate. What I knew was that whoever was negotiating on behalf of anybody in Zepa, whether soldier or civilian, was negotiating from a position of weakness. Further, I could see, and I can see it in these documents, that the military were not represented in this negotiating panel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. I understand you. But please tell us, did Torlak communicate with Avdo Palic and did he and Avdo Palic communicate with Alija Izetbegovic on a daily basis as you did? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea of the degree of communication between Torlak and Palic. And at the time, as opposed to now, I was aware that the -- Izetbegovic could communicate with the people in the enclaves. But to the degree of this and the frequency it was happening, I had no idea at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Yesterday we read out the letters and answers on the basis of everything we read out in the document, D55, page 30, the letter of Avdo Palic to Alija Izetbegovic. Do we not see on that basis that they have constant communication on a daily basis, and is Palic asking him to allow both the civilians and the soldiers to withdraw once certain requirements are met? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking -- I'm not entirely clear. Are you trying -- are you asking me what I understood at the time or are you asking me to comment on a document that you're now showing me? A document that I was not aware of at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith, for answering this. I am satisfied with your answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the witness asked you to clarify your question. He didn't provide you with any answer yet. He wanted to know what the essence of your question was, and therefore you should explain that to enable him to answer the question. Otherwise, it's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your assistance, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I asked whether Avdo Palic had communication on a daily basis and whether he communicated with regard to this particular event with Alija Izetbegovic. Did he ask for approval to be given for all the soldiers and inhabitants of Zepa to be evacuated from the enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, and the witness asked you to clarify if you want to have an answer about his knowledge at the time or if you want to have a comment of the witness reading the document now. This was the request of the witness. You should answer that and clarify that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: He can give a comment, he can say whatever he likes. I accept any answer he gives because he's a witness and I am the accused. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in that case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To overcome this situation --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I have answered his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should answer in both ways.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your understanding at that time and your interpretation of the documents.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I have explained already, I understood that there was communications between the enclaves and Sarajevo and that -- but the degree of this communication, I did not know at the time. What I'm now learning is that it was more comprehensive than I thought that it was at the time. And it would appear from what you have shown me that Palic wanted to get everyone out by helicopter. And I would go on with the comment that the point why he wanted to go out by helicopter in my understanding was to avoid passing through the Bosnian Serb military, who he did not trust. Particularly after the experience of the survivors of Srebrenica who had reached the Zepa enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is he writing that in his letter? Is he explicitly asking his president to carry out this exchange which would make it possible for them to leave the enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is asking them -- him to facilitate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now display 65 ter 2247. I don't remember the number actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Stop a moment, please. You can -- may check the number. And in the meantime, Judge Mindua has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Smith, I listened carefully to the questions and answers with General Tolimir relating to Mr. Torlak's ability to represent Avdo Palic and the Muslim military. For the time being I don't wish to address the weakness, as you called it, of the Bosnian army, or the Muslim side, to be more specific. But as far as Mr. Torlak is concerned, this person was a member of the War Presidency in the Zepa municipality. According to the document we have just seen, i.e., the agreement signed with General Mladic, if I have understood you correctly, you hesitate and you don't believe that Mr. Torlak was capable of representing the Muslim army. This is just a point of clarification. Are you aware of the prerogatives of the War Presidency in the municipality of Zepa, or is this a personal assessment on your part when you say that Torlak was in no legitimate position to represent Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not -- I have no memory and I don't think I ever was shown a formal statement, paper, or whatever of the relationship between War Presidencies and the Bosnian military. But what I'm about to say is a bit more than just comment; this is informed, if you like, by my observations at the time and my experience of how these matters get conducted more generally. Your -- the relationship between the civil and the military can become complex and very, very rarely are the military authorities directly subordinated to the civilian authorities all the way down the hierarchical chain of command. And the reason for this is that the military are handled and committed and used as an entity, as an entity of the state, while the civil arrangements are to deal with -- as they cascade down the hierarchy, are there to deal with the local issues. And you will find exactly the same thing happening in Bosnia. The armed forces are being controlled and committed and used on a state basis, Bosnian government basis, across the whole of their territory. And they are employing the armed forces in the enclaves as part of a greater plan. This isn't just a Zepa-related business that that military is undertaking. And, therefore, their command arrangements are held more centrally, and their local commander has a degree of latitude that is independent of the civil authorities in any -- in that locality. And that is why I do not accept that Torlak had the authority -- of course he was capable; he was clearly a capable leader of his community in those circumstances. But he didn't have the authority, and that is evident from some of the evidence we've been given where you see Izetbegovic indicating that he has other plans for the military and there are other possibilities for them to be used that are separate to the dealings with the civil population within that community. Does that answer the difference? Or answer your question about the difference?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If I have understood you correctly, you're saying that you did not more specifically read the legal texts that lay behind the setting up of the War Presidency in Zepa. And for the commander Avdo Palic to be tied by this agreement between Torlak and General Palic, he had to be present; or, if not, his military hierarchy should have been present, and the mere civilian Torlak was not sufficient in that case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I'm certainly saying that. I'd go further, that I don't actually have any great confidence in this agreement as it's been presented. We're making this signed as though this is being conducted in some office in some court between advocates. This is nothing of the sort. This Torlak and Co. have just had their community invaded, there are soldiers of the opposition all over the place, and they're now being asked to make an agreement. In English slang there is a saying that the large print giveth and the small print taketh away, and the -- this agreement is a good example of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Another question by Judge Nyambe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to understand the relationships between the people you dealt with in the context of these events. In paragraph 108 of the document on the screen it says that" following the meeting between General Smith and Hamdija Torlak." In what capacity were you meeting with him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My capacity is as command of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: No, on his part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't remember the specifics of that meeting, but if it's the one I -- if he's there up at the check-point at the place beginning with B, who I can't remember it now, he is representing the civil community. I understand that that is what his role is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: But quite clearly he's working very closely with Avdo Palic, because on the basis of information from your meeting, he's sent to this dramatic telegram or letter to the president. It seems to me that there's quite a link --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, I've no -- there's -- I'm trying to -- there's no doubt that they were communicating, and it was in the interests of the Bosnian Serbs to ensure that they communicated. Indeed, I asked to see Palic. I was never allowed to see him. I wanted to talk to him too. But it's -- the central point, in addition to the one I've made to you, that there was a separate arrangement of command and authority in these circumstances and why, is that one group of people, Torlak, is representing the civil community and the women and children, and Palic is representing the -- all those men of military age, and there is a distinct difference to how they anticipated they would be dealt with, particularly after the reports of what happened in Srebrenica had reached them. And it had reached them and they knew much more about what had happened in Srebrenica at this stage than I did because survivors from the Srebrenica enclave had reached Zepa by that stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NYAMBE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So now, bearing in mind everything that you said, tell us, did Avdo Palic represent a military dictatorship in Zepa or did he recognise Torlak as the member of the War Presidency and the president of the Executive Board of the municipality? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Palic did not represent a military dictatorship. And I -- as far as I'm aware, he recognised Torlak as being a member of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are going to take a look at P736. P736. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And while we are waiting for it, we are going to see what was the function of Mr. Torlak and other members of the War Presidency. This is a decision written by the War Presidency and forwarded on the 27th to the military commanders. So it says at the beginning: "The War Presidency of the Zepa municipality at its meeting held on the 27th of July, 1995, attended by Mehmed Hajric, president of the War Presidency; Hamdija Torlak, president of the Executive Committee; and Amir Imamovic, commander of the civil protection staff, hereby adopt the following decision." Now I'm reading the decision itself: "All able-bodied men from 18 to 55 years of age shall surrender their weapons to the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska in the presence of UNPROFOR at the UNPROFOR base in Zepa. All able-bodied men shall be registered by the ICRC and shall be guarded by the forces of the VRS in the presence of UNPROFOR in Zepa until an agreement on exchange has been reached. "Following the agreement on exchange, and exchange of POWs, all able-bodied men registered by the ICRC shall be safely escorted by UNPROFOR and evacuated to a territory of their free choice. "Urgently inform the Muslim authorities in Sarajevo about this decision and carry it out immediately. "In Zepa on the 27th of July, 1995." Signed by Rajko Kusic, the commander of the Rogatica Brigade. Lieutenant-Colonel Sejmon Dudnjik was supposed to certify it, but he didn't sign it, as well as Ratko Mladic. And it was also signed by the three members of the War Presidency: Mehmed Hajric, the president; Hamdija Torlak, member of the Presidency; and Amir Imamovic, member of the Presidency. So based on this, my question is: Did you have an opportunity to find out who the members of the War Presidency were? And did you meet anybody else besides Torlak on Boksanica during the day of the 27th of July? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall whether I was there on the 27th or not. I certainly met -- it is probable I was there on the 27th but I don't recall the dates. I met others, other members of the civil leadership, or people I believed to be other members of the civil leadership other than Torlak, but I don't remember the names of them. And by the 27th, if I had been shown this document on the 27th, my reaction was that it had been written while the -- and signed under duress. This was not something that those people were in any position not to agree to sign. The -- Zepa was completely in the hands of the Bosnian Serbs at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, while you were the commander of UNPROFOR in Bosnia, was that agreement signed under the pressure and the threat of the use of air force against those who wouldn't sign the agreement? Were any threats of the similar nature used also during the conference in Rambouillet, during the negotiations between the delegation of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Kosovo delegation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've lost me. We've moved out of Zepa? Is this question relating to Zepa or are we now talking generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This question pertains to Zepa, because the losing side always signs an agreement under certain circumstances while the winning side signs the same agreement under different circumstances; isn't that true? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall any threat or use of air power in relation to Zepa and the negotiations and so forth that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that Yugoslavia was bombed during three months in order for it to accept the Rambouillet agreement, an agreement that was imposed by the NATO so that Yugoslavia would have to accept the war of the rebels under the conditions defined by the NATO? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no question that General Smith is capable of answering the question. My only request is that we, for the record, put a date, a year, on the events we're talking about. I think we all remember, generally, Rambouillet and so forth, but just for the record so we can orient ourselves to time, place, I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, can you help Mr. Thayer by giving a time-frame.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I will pose a different question. Mr. Smith, were you the UNPROFOR commander in Bosnia at the time when the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was bombed and certain events occurred in Kosovo? Thank you. More precisely we are talking about 1978.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Um ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I meant 1999.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We appear to be talking about 1999, a completely and a different set of circumstances to that that was occurring in Zepa in 1995. And I was not the commander of UNPROFOR in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where were you in 1999 during the bombardment of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Because Kosovo decided to secede. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the deputy supreme allied commander Europe based in the NATO headquarters at Mons in Belgium.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember whether force was used at the time in order to achieve political agreements? I mean, force against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And after they didn't want to sign the agreement in Rambouillet, were they bombed during the period of three months in 1999? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Force was used in 1999 over Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I'm not sure if we are dealing with the Kosovo conflict in this trial. You should focus on what the witness can provide you with, his knowledge and his involvement in 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I didn't speak about Kosovo for Kosovo sake; I was addressing a principle. When two sides have to reach an agreement, the victorious side and the losing side, we have a certain situation. We can compare it even with Libya. Those who have the force are able to impose the conditions which will then regulate the cease-fire agreement in Libya. Currently NATO countries are conducting an air-strikes campaign in Libya. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you are -- that was not a question. And, indeed, I repeat, you should focus on the substance of this trial. The witness is not here as an expert witness about political negotiations and the involvement of the military all over the world. He is a fact witness about the conflict in Bosnia. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you claim that Torlak was compelled, forced - I'm not quite sure which words you used - to sign that agreement. Can you tell us, did the Muslim agreement accept -- did the Muslim government accept the agreement to evacuate the civilian population and able-bodied men under a condition that an exchange would be organised? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think the Muslim government did accept that the population would be evacuated under a condition of an exchange. I don't recall that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have again D55, document entitled "The Fall of Zepa" written by a Prosecution expert. I would like to take a look at page 28, paragraph 102, and the second segment of that paragraph. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we can see paragraph 102. And I would like to take a look at the segment written in smaller font. I quote -- Or maybe first I should quote the top of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could the smaller font be brought up one size larger for me, please. Brilliant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So let us read out the whole paragraph, 102: "While negotiations between the VRS and ABiH delegations regarding the people in Zepa were going on in Sarajevo. On the 25th of July, Lieutenant-Colonel Jovica Karanovic updated General Tolimir on the situation at the negotiations as follows: Muslim government accepts the proposed (signed) agreement in its entirety on condition that both civilians and able-bodied men are evacuated together from the enclave of Zepa. In order to sign this agreement, Muslims are willing to secure release of all prisoners of war demanded by VRS. (It was not stated precisely when and how they are going to release them, remark by JK)." So this is what Mr. Bezruchenko, the OTP investigator, wrote based in the document quoted in the footnote 156. We can find ERN number of the relevant document in that footnote. So my question is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please slow down. Please slow down a bit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: My question is: Did the Muslim government arrive at the negotiations with the position that they were going to accept the agreement signed in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they -- what their opinion was or their plan was. What you're showing me is a report by one of your staff to you. I don't know what that tells me about the Muslims and their position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a negotiator who was present at the airport together with the UNPROFOR representatives, and he reported about what was going on at the Sarajevo airport. So could you please tell us, were you aware of the fact that there were negotiations at the Sarajevo airport between the Muslim government and the delegation sent by the VRS? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, when the accused refers to a negotiator who was present at the airport together with the UNPROFOR representatives, could we have some clarification of to whom he was referring. There are a number of people referred to in this paragraph 102, including Mr. Karanovic as well as others, in the smaller font text. So when he is referring to a negotiator, who is he referring to? Just so we know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It would be helpful for the witness to know to whom you are referring. Can you give the name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Yes, I can. In line 2 of paragraph 102, we find that Lieutenant-Colonel Jovica Karanovic updated General Tolimir of the situation at the negotiations. So it was Bezruchenko who quoted Karanovic's words in this document that he wrote and that is entitled "The Fall of Zepa," an overview of military events. So my question is: Can we see from this document that negotiations were conducted in Sarajevo, and did you know that the representative of UNPROFOR was present about these negotiations which pertained to the situation in Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said, I know, I think I said it yesterday, that these negotiations about prisoner exchange were going on and that these were facilitated by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, do you know who was present during these negotiations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know who the UNPROFOR representative was on a day-to-day basis, but it would have been from the civil affairs people in either headquarters of Sector Sarajevo or my headquarters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you know who was present on behalf of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, your colloquy with the General may have answered my question, but the question still stands. When he's referring to a negotiator, is he talking about Karanovic, Bugojno, Bulajic? There are five or six names that are referenced here when he refers to a negotiator as being the source of the information or of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I read two times. You can find it in paragraph 102 in the second sentence. It was Lieutenant Jovica Karanovic who sent to General Tolimir on the 25th of July the following updated report of negotiations. I don't know whether you heard what I quoted. I simply repeated what was written in the paragraph. I didn't mention Bulajic or anybody else in my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please continue with your next question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let us move on to another group of questions. What was the perspective of Sarajevo, chronologically speaking, on the events in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have 2247. 65 ter 2247. Thank you. Thank you. We have it on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It's an outgoing code cable sent to Annan, United Nations New York, and the sender is Akashi. The subject is a meeting between President Izetbegovic and General Smith on the 17th of July, 1995. Did you meet Alija Izetbegovic on that day as we can find it in the subject line of this code cable? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If that code cable says I did, then I probably did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at page 4 so that the witness can see what my questions are going to be, related to this document. It's page 3 in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to quote from the first part of the first paragraph. Or rather, first I'm going too read out the title. "Meeting, President Izetbegovic/General Smith, 17 July 1995." I quote: "The meeting took place at the Presidency at 1050 hours on the 17th of July, 1995, at President Izetbegovic's urgent request. Izetbegovic expressed interest in UNPROFOR's capability to evacuate the civilian population of Zepa if necessary. General Smith explained that there would be few logistical problems but obviously any evacuation would require BSA consent. Izetbegovic stated that there were two categories of people in Zepa: Firstly, the sick, wounded, and elderly; and then the rest of the population. He asked what could be done to ensure the safety of at least the first category. Izetbegovic asked General Smith to make contact with the Serbs and find out their conditions for the safe evacuation of the civilian population of Zepa. General Smith agreed to pass the query to the Serbs immediately." My question: Do you remember this meeting now? Do you remember that it was on Alija Izetbegovic's request that you begin to study the possibility of the evacuation of the wounded and civilian population from Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refreshes my memory of the substance of the meeting, yes. I'd like to read the whole document before answering further questions. How many pages does it run to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The document contains four pages, I was told. It will consume some time and that would be possible during the break perhaps. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's really a page and a half of text. It's four if you count the two sort of cover pages. But the actual text is fairly -- fairly short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, if you want to deal with this document with the witness, I think we should give him a hard copy of it and have the first break now to enable the witness to read the full text and then you may put your questions in relation to this document to the witness. Are you in agreement with that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I accept your proposal. I think that it is necessary for the witness to know what exactly were the topics of his discussion with Alija Izetbegovic before he can answer my questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: A hard copy of this document should be given to the witness. We must have our first break now. And we will resume five minutes before 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, I believe you read the document. Based on it and based on what I could read in the first paragraph, I'd like to ask you this: On the 17th was there a meeting between you and Alija Izetbegovic and did he task you to determine what the appropriate safe measures needed to be in place to safely evacuate the civilian population from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was this meeting, and he wanted me to see what we could do as UNPROFOR to help evacuate the population of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since it was always important for you to know the position of one side, was it a clear position during this meeting put forth by Alija Izetbegovic that he wished to see the entire civilian population evacuated from Zepa as of that date?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted to see the population evacuated, with particular reference to the sick, wounded, and elderly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you convey this wish of his to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does the text of the document as drafted by your associates clearly and accurately reflect the message you conveyed?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are referring to the -- the bit in inverted commas, "I have been asked by the Bosnian government" and following on from that, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Precisely. Did you convey the Bosnian government position to the VRS as stated here?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That message was sent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it clear from that message that the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo represented by Alija Izetbegovic wished the civilian population from Zepa evacuated to territory held by the Federation?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it -- I'm quite clear that that is what he wanted. He wanted them to be safely evacuated in the circumstances of Zepa at the time. Or from the circumstances of Zepa at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If you recall the document we saw which was titled, "The Agreement on the Disarming of the Military Able-Bodied Men from Zepa," we then looked at items 2, 5, and 7. Did item 7 of the document reflect Alija Izetbegovic's requests about the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember item 7 in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should have it on --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We should have it back on the screen. Mr. Tolimir, we have seen two agreements today. Please indicate which one you want to have on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is the agreement and the item 7 I refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will quote: "In accordance with the Geneva Conventions of 12 August 1949 and the additional protocols of 1977, the civilian population of Zepa shall be given the freedom to choose their place of residence while hostilities continue." Thank you. Does item 7 of the agreement clearly put forth Alija Izetbegovic's wish when he asked you to convey that position of his and his request to the VRS?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it doesn't. Not precisely. And these -- your -- we are looking at a document that's signed, I think it's six days -- on the 24th of July, while the other document you've produced for me to look at is on the 17th of July. The -- what it says in paragraph 7 of the document on the screen, the agreement of the 24th of July, it says that the people will be allowed to choose.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Alija Izetbegovic ask for the same thing? What is the difference between item 7 and his request?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis of the request is that it is about their evacuation. The assumption is that they have chosen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at item 7 on the screen, you can see that it invokes the Geneva Conventions and its protocols. In its last sentence, it reads that they "shall be given the freedom to choose their place of residence while hostilities continue." In that sense it goes beyond the conventions, because I don't believe we can find this in International Humanitarian Law and the Laws of War. This sentence expressly states that the status as such would be enjoyed until or for as long as hostilities continue.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that phrase is used in that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the residents of Zepa who had lived there before the war now actually reside in Zepa again?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that the -- that one of the signatories of the agreement testified to that effect, having said so in his testimony in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see here whether the Bosnian government undertook all practical measures, including appointing representatives who would be in charge of the evacuation, so that those representatives could liaise with representatives of the VRS about the issue?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]We can see that on page 4. And we should go back to 224 so that the witness can see it. Actually, 2247.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are referring to the document 65 ter 2247, I assume. And just for the record --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] [no interpretation] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record -- I am talking. I am talking. Please don't interrupt me. For the record, the last document, the agreement, on the screen was D51. Now we have this document again on the screen. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. It wasn't my intention to interrupt you. I actually received a question in the interpretation I received; that's why I started answering. In any case, let us look at page 4 of the agreement of the 17th of July, 1995. Paragraph 2. Paragraph 2, please. It should be page 4 in the Serbian version so that I could peruse it as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, this is page 4 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the - first, second, third, fourth - fifth paragraph in the English, but we don't see the fourth page in Serbian. Please change the page from 1 to 4. We can see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I quote: "General Smith passed Mladic's offer to the Bosnian government. The president appeared initially amenable to the idea and nominated General Muslimovic and Mr. Ljevakovic as his representatives. These names were passed to Mladic, who appeared content with them, and arrangements were set in train." My question is this: Did the Muslim side, on the 17th, when the meeting between you and Alija Izetbegovic took place, appoint these negotiators so that they could negotiate the way civilians would be evacuated from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: They nominated those two names and then these were withdrawn later in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it VRS responsibility, or did the Muslim government withdraw their nominations?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I said the -- during the afternoon, the Bosnian government backtracked on this proposal and declined to send any representative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 6 -- sorry, 4 of this document, we can see that General Mladic said that they had to stop all fighting and that they had to hand over all of their weapons. Can you find that sentence on the page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate where the witness should find it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the Serbian it is on page 4 out of 6. In the first paragraph. In the English it follows the quote. It's around the middle of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see where it says at the bottom of the page in English "a second call was made to Mladic." Is that where we are?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think it could be the paragraph in the middle of the page. The paragraph -- yes, indeed, you can see the quote there. "Mladic then offered safe passage to any representative." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. But I thought the question was about having to hand over weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have page 4 in e-court, the first paragraph in Serbian, so that I could indicate what portion of the text I was referring to. This is the first page. I need page 4, please. This is the first out of seven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, the numbering of the pages is always a problem. Are you referring to the page number of the document itself, this message about the meetings, or to the number of the e-court page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I don't know what the pagination is in e-court but I think it ought to be page 4 of the document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think your assistant will be able to help you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There seems to be a problem. But in the English version it should be the fourth paragraph in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The penultimate sentence reads: "Mladic asked that all fighting cease and all weapons be handed over." Was this a legitimate request by General Mladic to have the zone demilitarised since he -- his intention was to allow the entire civilian population to move to BiH-held territory?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, indeed we have, still, a problem. It should be the next page in B/C/S and not page 4. But I don't find this quote.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. It is page 6 in B/C/S. In English it is page 4 most likely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And where can we find it? Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think General Smith had it correct, that I believe what General Tolimir is paraphrasing is the last -- oh, now we have to go back in the English version. We had it on the screen. It's the last paragraph, last full sentence, that begins with his reply. And it's just after the line that General Smith quoted. "A second call was made to Mladic." So it's the very bottom of this page. It does continue to the next page in English. I believe that's what General Tolimir is quoting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this assistance. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir. What is, in fact, your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I was not paraphrasing. I'm reading from the last sentence we see on the screen on page 6, the last sentence of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Indjic said that it meant that before the civilians are allowed to leave and other issues began to be resolved, all fighting needed to cease and all weapons had to be handed over." My question is this: Was this a legitimate request by the VRS and by Mladic, having in mind that this entire zone was supposed to be vacated of any civilians, and their condition was for the armed forces to lay down their weapons?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I have a big problem with this kind of examination. We need a clear reference where we can find the portion you are reading from. I don't find it. The witness will not be able to find it. Perhaps because he has a hard copy he is in a better position. But to follow your conduct of the cross-examination, it is really necessary to give a clear reference and indication where we can find these portions, in English and in B/C/S. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Since Mr. Thayer wanted to go back one page in English, now we should go one page forward so that the witness could see the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which part of this document are you quoting from? This is a clear question. Please give us a reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am quoting the first sentence you see in the English version at the top of the screen, that is, the very end of that paragraph. It is asked that all fighting stopped and all weapons be handed over.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I will repeat my question. Was this a legitimate request by the army allowing the entire civilian population to leave to Bosnia-Herzegovina-held territory and asking at the same time that all able-bodied men hand down their weapons and stop fighting? Was this a legitimate military request?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a negotiating position. It's neither -- it's not -- it's what he wanted. There's no -- and what he's saying he wants is that he has disarmed the Bosnian army in the pocket and then he would allow the civil population to leave. It's a condition. Hostilities are to end and then the population can go. That's what I understand is his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I am asking you this: As UNPROFOR commander, was it a legitimate request to allow to leave -- allow the population to leave alongside all able-bodied men but that all able-bodied men should lay down their weapons first? Was this a legitimate request made by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he's -- he calls them civilians. And I'm not in a position to say whether it's legitimate or not. It hasn't happened. This is, as I say, is a negotiating position.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was UNPROFOR supposed to carry out demilitarisation of Zepa? Did General Mladic warn you of the fact that the zone had not been demilitarised as envisaged under the agreement? Perhaps you recall that so that we don't need to go back to the specific document.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: UNPROFOR was not supposed to carry out demilitarisation. And I'm not clear what agreement you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was the area of Zepa supposed to have been demilitarised in keeping with the agreement on demilitarisation of Zepa and Srebrenica signed by Sefer Halilovic and Ratko Mladic in 1993? On behalf of UNPROFOR it was Philippe Morillon who signed it.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the absolute details of that agreement. But I think you're correct; the word "demilitarisation" does appear in that, or did appear in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us, was this a legitimate request by the VRS to ask for a demilitarisation exercise to be conducted before all -- before the entire population left so that there would be no possibility left for them to carry out any further attacks against Serb-held territory?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't asking. Mladic, in this document that is on the screen, is not asking for demilitarisation. He's asking for one side to lay down all their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand your answer. Please look at the penultimate paragraph on the page you have in English. It is the last paragraph in Serbian. It reads as follows: "The Bosnian government rejected Mladic's conditions. In particular their requirement to surrender all weapons as a precursor to the start of negotiations." My question is this: Who was obstructing the implementation of the agreement we saw at the beginning signed on the 24th? We referred to item 7 of that agreement a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the answer because this conversation -- these conversations that are being recorded are taking place on the 17th of July, which is some days before the document that you referred me to, and included the paragraph 7 with the Geneva Conventions mentioned in it, was signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did the negotiations begin prior to that and were you notified?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which -- what is that? Did the negotiations prior to what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Before the conversation you had with Alija Izetbegovic. Or was Alija Izetbegovic the one who initiated this idea that all civilians should cross over to Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who initiated the idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you convey his idea to the VRS after the 17th when you had that conversation with him?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I -- well, again, it was his request that I conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does it mean that Alija Izetbegovic was the one who came up with the idea of evacuating the entire civilian population of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you whether that was the case or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you merely some kind of test pilot for Alija Izetbegovic for him to test what the feelings of the other side were when he asked you to convey that message?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you what he thought my role was. I could -- you have before you a document describing what I did in response to his request.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. This request of his, was it merely a way to test the position of the VRS, or did he have serious intentions in stating that he wanted to see the entire civilian population evacuated from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that he was concerned and gave me every impression of being concerned as to the safety of the civil population of Zepa. What his other motivations were, I cannot tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, was the evacuation of the population from Zepa carried out in accordance with the agreement that had been signed between the representatives of Zepa and the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see D51. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see this document yet again. Did the evacuations start, of the civilian population from Zepa, in accordance with the provisions of this agreement that had been signed by the representatives of the civilian authorities and the War Presidency in Zepa with the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The actual course of the evacuation of the population and the dates on which it occurred, I don't -- the precise, you know, what days buses left and so forth, I would need to look at the reporting of the time. The -- my memory is that it did not go entirely according to this document. And I don't think the ICRC, for example, ran the -- I'm almost certain they didn't run a holding centre and so forth. So I don't think paragraph 8 was carried out, for example. Nor was 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. I understand your position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at document D55 again now. Page 105. Because you had just asked to see how it was that the evacuation had started. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please don't move to the next document. Judge Mindua has a question for the witness in relation to the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Smith, sir, I would like to understand this question better, i.e., the evacuation of civilians mentioned in this Exhibit D55, in paragraph 7. The Defence, from what I understand, would like to show another document. Since I have this document, document 51 before me, I would like to clarify the situation. According to this paragraph, the civilian population will be permitted to choose its place of residence - I'm translating the document directly from the French - whilst the hostilities are still on-going. What I'm interested in is the end of the hostilities right now. I know that in terms of International Humanitarian Law the evacuation of civilians is not mandatory but is encouraged. I'm referring to Article 17 of the 4th Geneva Convention. Of course, military commanders cannot expose civilians to danger when the latter are in the battle-field. This is why I understand this provision full well which gets a party to agree on the evacuation of the civilian population as is mentioned in paragraph 7 as the hostilities are still on-going. This is my question: According to you, when did the hostilities cease? I'm talking about the hostilities in particular and in Bosnia in general.
