Do you have any idea on what date the hostilities ceased?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me -- the formal ending of the hostilities occurred in -- on a date in October 1995 when there was a cease-fire agreed by all parties. Again, I'd have to look at the record to give you the date, but my memory is it's somewhere around about the middle of October. In the specific case, and here I won't use the word "hostilities" between the parties, there was, in the immediate vicinity of the major population and the civil point population in Zepa and the village of Zepa, there was no fighting taking place at and around the time of the 24th of July. And I don't recall reporting of actual fighting taking place around this village in the immediate vicinity of that area in the enclave of Zepa from certainly after the London conference and my return from that. The Bosnian Serb army was in -- was occupying and in firm control of that vicinity and everything that was going on in that area. The -- there was no evidence of armed Bosnian army personnel at the bottom of the hill where the village was or up at the top of the hill where the check-point was and where I was. The only armed men I saw were either UN soldiers under my command or those of the Bosnian Serb army. And there was no fighting taking place. Does that draw the distinction between the actual combat going on as opposed to the hostilities as a whole?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you very much. I have understood this well. You talked about the official date of the ending of the hostilities and you also discussed the situation on the ground and you said that there was no fighting, in fact. So according to you, if you can answer this question, if you can't, it doesn't matter, why was this sentence introduced in this paragraph? What I mean is, "the civilian population must choose its place of residence whilst the hostilities are still on-going." Why do we have this part of the sentence, "while the hostilities are still on-going"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an observation of my experience at the time, reinforced to some extent by seeing documents subsequently by attending this court that I didn't know existed or didn't -- hadn't seen at the time in 1995. But both parties were in the habit of sprinkling their argumentation in these various meetings and in documents that, as I say, I've now seen, with these phrases appealing to some other authority such as the Geneva Conventions or so forth. And I came to some extent to ignore them because you found that they weren't being used, once I'd started to find out what that convention was or treaty was in some historical case and so on and so forth, this was being referred to in a very self-serving and partial way. And I came to find that this was a habit of all parties in this affair. And I'm not surprised to find a paragraph in there that doesn't actually -- in my memory of reading the Geneva Conventions, I'm not entirely sure that the beginning of the sentence is actually connected with the end of the sentence in any logical sense or fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please carry on. And I have a request. Sometimes you are putting your questions with a very loud voice to the witness. There's no need for that because we all have our microphones and earphones and everybody will understand you. Please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I put the microphone away and then I was asked to speak into the microphone, but this is just the way I speak. I would like to thank Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: You claim here that there were no clashes in the enclave. 1D617 is the document that we looked at yesterday. May I remind you of that. And let me just show you that is General Mladic's letter sent to you personally on the 10th of July, 1995. Let us just read what General Mladic wrote to you, why there was a conflict in the enclave. I'm sorry that we have to read the document again, but what you said just now was that there were no conflicts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P185. Thank you both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think everybody understood what General Smith said in his answer and in particular the time-period to which he was referring. We are now about to reread a letter that predates this by two weeks. General Tolimir can ask the questions he wishes and we don't want to place restrictions on the subject matter within certain -- certain obvious guide-lines, but that's not what General Smith testified to. He testified that at a particular time the fighting had stopped. So showing him a letter from ten days earlier, I think, is really going to waste time on this issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for this assistance, but it is the conduct of the cross-examination. You may deal with that in re-examination. Mr. Tolimir, what is your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, do you remember that we looked at this document yesterday? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you remember that General Mladic in paragraph 2 of this document wrote the following to you: "I'm reminding you that since then to the present day Muslim forces by way of attacks and sabotage terrorist groups killed 100 and wounded over 200 Serb civilians. They torched several Serb villages in the immediate vicinity of the zone, committing unheard of massacres against the civilian population. Over the past few days they conducted a large-scale military operation in order to link the enclave in the area of Zepa -- with the villages in the Zepa area and they torched the villages of Visnjica and Banja Lucica and they killed the entire population. In carrying out their dastardly intentions, they did not spare even the members of UNPROFOR. Although your forces protected them, they were their victims themselves." Was this sent to you before the combat in Zepa took place actually?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: If what you've put on that screen says all that and it's dated, I think, on the 9th of - is it? - 10th of July, as I think I answered last time, I'm on leave when this arrives, but I am quite prepared to believe that it was read and understood in my headquarters. And on my return it would have been included in my briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Upon returning from leave were you informed that the conflict had escalated between the Muslim soldiers in the Zepa enclave and the Army of Republika Srpska around the Zepa enclave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: My briefing was centred on the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you whether you had been informed about conflicts taking place in Zepa between the Muslim army that was supposed to be demilitarised and the Army of Republika Srpska that was around the demilitarised zone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The -- I knew that this fighting was going on, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the basis of what are you claiming, then, that the Army of Republika Srpska acted unlawfully and that it occupied Zepa if there was fighting in that zone and General Mladic had warned that he would turn it into a demilitarised zone because it was not actually demilitarised as stated in this letter that read out to you because there was no translation for you to read?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you claiming ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I was told that there is now an English translation. It was sent to the Registry today. And this will help you to put your questions accordingly. But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm -- I am claiming and stating because of the evidence of my own eyes that the army of the Bosnian Serbs had occupied Zepa and that -- to go back a whole range of questions, and that the -- there was no fighting taking place on and around the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could the English version please be enlarged.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Before this letter was sent, was the Army of Republika Srpska in the territory of the enclave of Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter of the 10th of July, the Bosnian Serb army was not in the safe area of Zepa, as far as I was aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. The military operations of the Army of Republika Srpska against Zepa, did they take place because they had killed 100 and wounded 200 civilians around the demilitarised zone as armed groups left the demilitarised zone? That is what General Mladic is referring to in paragraph 2 of this letter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: He -- if I -- can I have the page turned, please, on my ... My understanding of this is that he is complaining of the Bosnian military operating out of Srebrenica, not out of Zepa. He is saying that they're starting operations with a view to linking up with the enclave in Zepa. He is not saying that people from Zepa have attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I don't want to waste time with a single document, and the Trial Chamber actually has several documents about Zepa. I understand your position. You know when the evacuations started and how that happened.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before that, I'm just going to ask for D55 to be displayed in e-court, paragraph 101, on page 27. This document has to do with the fall of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: It was written up by Mr. Bezruchenko for the OTP. He was sent by your command to Zepa before it surrendered. Thank you. This is what Mr. Bezruchenko says in paragraph 101 that both you and I can see on our screens. This is what he says: "President Izetbegovic on the 25th of July in his letter to the Security Council requested UNPROFOR to assist the safe evacuation of civilians. The Security Council at once responded positively through a presidential statement." And then he provides that document in footnote 154 and he provides the ERN number of that document, as you can see too, down there in that footnote, 154. This is my question --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we read just one more sentence. Can we have the next page in Serbian. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: "Intensive negotiations then took place between General Smith and General Mladic over conditions and modalities of such an operation." Now, this is my question: Through a presidential statement did the Security Council authorise you to carry out the evacuation of the civilian population of Zepa in line with Alija Izetbegovic's request, and were you informed of that decision? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the actions of the Security Council. I had forgotten about that completely. But I was fully engaged in doing just that at the time, so I don't -- I don't suppose I felt that it was anything more than an added authority from my political masters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. At the time, because you cannot recall now, were you duty-bound as UNPROFOR commander to abide by the presidential statement of the Security Council? So could you please tell the Trial Chamber what that means, "presidential statement." What is its form and content and how binding is it for UN forces, in this case UNPROFOR? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm no expert in this. My understanding is that there is a procedure within the United Nations where the president of the Security Council can issue a statement without calling the complete Security Council into session. He does this when he is confident that there is no likelihood of disagreement on the council. He does it so that the authorities of the and statements by the Security Council are timely and authoritative. Its impact on the -- on military operations would merely reinforce the importance of achieving this particular objective. It would be more, as it were, setting the context for one's military operation rather than changing the operation itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. Do you know that presidential statements are issued after Security Council sessions and that the president of the Security Council as chairman is duty-bound to present the decisions and conclusions reached either by way of a statement or a resolution? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know it in that form, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us whether presidential statements were binding on the parties, and did UNPROFOR had to implement them in accordance with Security Council instructions? Did your command receive the presidential statement of the Security Council where he responds favourably to Alija Izetbegovic's request to have the civilian population moved out of Zepa to BH-controlled territory? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I doubt that we did receive the statement in the way you've expressed it as though it was an order. As I say, it's something that would have set the context in which we were operating, and we were already doing what the Security Council was urging us to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have this document in Serbian version. I would like to see the previous page so that we can see the footnote 155 both in Serbian and in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So now we can see footnote -- actually, I meant 154 and not 155. And it says: "UNPROFOR HQ Sarajevo. Office of civil affairs. Weekly situation report number 129, 24 to the 30th of July, 1995." So was this statement provided to you, to your command, and to your civilian sector who was subordinated -- which was subordinated to you? And then they send two of their representatives to Zepa, Mr. Edward Joseph and Mr. Bezruchenko. Thank you. And he is actually the person who wrote this.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have referred me to a document by headquarters, civil affairs office of UNPROFOR, headquarters in Sarajevo. Is this where the presidential statement is appearing? Well, I'm -- or have we moved away from this presidential statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, we haven't moved from the presidential statement. I asked you whether it was binding for all the sides and UNPROFOR, and you said that you were involved in carrying out those activities. You also said that you did not remember the contents of this statement. That is why I reminded you about what you did at the time. Immediately after that you contacted General Mladic and began carrying out the presidential statement in practice; isn't that so? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- told you, I don't recall the presidential statement. You have referred me to a document that is -- emanates apparently from my headquarters, not anything that has been passed down to me by a superior headquarters. And as we've seen from various reporting, by the -- by this time we have been engaged in the business of Zepa and its civil population for some days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question just to understand better. Were Mr. Joseph and Mr. Bezruchenko subordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not formally. They were part of the civil affairs staff, and I can't -- I think they are both part of Sector Sarajevo's civil affairs team. They are not part of my headquarters for UNPROFOR. But I may have been wrong there. At this stage I do not have a chief of civil affairs. I haven't had one since sometime in April. Mr. Pedauye doesn't appear on the scene until a little later, in either July or August. My -- and in many ways I am dealing direct with Sector Sarajevo's civil staff, as well as those that do not have a chief, in my own headquarters. I am -- I believe, I think initially, on the initiative of David Harland, but it may not have been, Joseph and Bezruchenko, he is -- they go into Zepa before we have presidential statements and so forth. Again, I can't give you the dates precisely, but they're there very early on in this event. And I don't understand the questions as to why this particular document that's being referred to in the footnote may mention a presidential statement having been made but it isn't any way an authority. This document looks to me as though it's the weekly situation report, and, in fact, that's what it says it is, sorry, for the week 24th-30th of July. So it was probably written at the end of July and not right at the end of the month. And I suspect it merely has an account that this statement was issued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you recall who were the superiors or the superior of Mr. Joseph and Mr. Bezruchenko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I say, I think, in a formal sense, it would have been Mr. Akashi back in Zagreb. But in the circumstances of Sarajevo at the time, I was -- knew perfectly well that these two had been sent into Sarajevo -- into Zepa, and to all intents and purposes I would have been their superior and directing what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would like to ask the witness to say whether the Security Council would issue a presidential statement without Alija Izetbegovic requesting it as one of the warring parties. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer for the thinking in the Security Council or the UN headquarters in New York at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. I asked you this because it is said that the Security Council requested UNPROFOR to help in the safe evacuation of the civilians. My question is: If the Security Council requested it, if you then undertook certain efforts, because we see here a mention of a discussion between General Smith and General Mladic, and if that evacuation had indeed commenced, can then General Tolimir be held responsible for simply carrying out the tasks that were defined by this agreement bearing in mind that he was simply part of a Main Staff in a similar way to which you were a commander in your staff? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, please switch off your microphone, otherwise we have the noise of your papers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I've said to you, I don't see that the -- we in UNPROFOR - and I separate UNPROFOR from the Bosnian Serb army at this stage, and every other army for that matter - we in UNPROFOR are already concerned with and setting out to deal with the evacuation of the civilians from Zepa. The fact that the Security Council then encourages to do this is, as I say, sets the context, sets the political urgency of doing this, but it is -- that is what it does. It doesn't alter what I am doing on anything. Now, whether or not you, General Tolimir, are part of the staff, an assistant commander of one of the armies engaged in this war, have a responsibility, I leave that to others to decide. You were there and you were conducting the -- a part of what went on in that enclave. That I can vouch for.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I know that I carried out what was agreed between you and General Mladic and the other warring party.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 65 ter 7247. That's the statement by this witness. I would like to take a look at page 20, paragraph 5, the first and the second sentence. Thank you. Can we also have the version -- can we also have the version in Serbian. It's page 20, paragraph 5, lines 1 and 2. It's the previous page in English. Thank you. It's the last paragraph, beginning with the words "General Tolimir."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So this is what you say. I quote from the Serbian version: "General Tolimir clearly played an important role at Zepa and appeared to be in charge of the cleansing of the pocket and the movement of civilians out of the pocket." My question is: Does that mean that all the representatives of UNPROFOR who took part in the negotiations were also in charge of cleansing of Zepa and the movement of civilians out of the pocket? You also said in examination-in-chief that I played an important role by providing the buses. So what I'm saying here is did I do all this in accordance with the negotiations and the agreement, or did I cleanse the enclave in a military sense? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are confusing deliberately or otherwise the creation of the situation with dealing with the situation, it having been created. As far as I am concerned, evacuating the population is a consequence of a situation that was created by you and the Bosnian Serb army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, if you finished your answer. Can you tell us now, was my activity in Zepa the consequence of the agreement signed by the two parties as we saw today in the documents that we looked at today? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I make my point, the agreement that you showed me on the screen was reached as a result of your attack into the safe area of Zepa, and the -- and the evacuation of the civil population then followed from that. And it followed from that in particular because of the experience of previous events, not least that in Srebrenica. And I think we've seen reference to my saying to General Mladic that I -- that we needed to evacuate the people, and this to be seen, and this is why the CNN got in, so that there was the least likelihood of any threat to the civil population occurring in the light of the -- what was beginning to be clear had occurred elsewhere and in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you stated that I gathered the buses. My question is: Is it possible that an assistant commander would go around finding buses in a unit two levels below the Main Staff, or would it be something normally carried out at the brigade level? In other words, would a commander do something like that or would it be entrusted to assistant commanders? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say you had gathered the buses. I said that it had been reported to me that you had taken people off a bus. And this is referred to in the document you've got on the screen somewhere. I've just seen it. Yes, there you are, in the very of paragraph you've referred me to. Second sentence: "I was told he personally removed 11 wounded males from the buses to an uncertain [Realtime transcript read in error "Albanian"] fate." Not "Albanian fate," to a "uncertain fate."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We can see that in this paragraph on page 20 of Bezruchenko's report. It's the second paragraph from the bottom in Serbian, and I think that it is also the second paragraph from the bottom in English. However, do you know when those combatants were taken off the buses? Can we find it in this paragraph? Also, did that happen after the Muslims refused to surrender their weapons? Take a look at the last paragraph where it says the 30th of July. That's the last paragraph in English and also the last paragraph in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: We're referring to my statement still, are we? Or the report on Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm referring to your statement, because you said that I took some men off the buses. Now I'm asking you, when were they taken off the buses? Were they able-bodied men? And were they taken off the buses only after the Muslim side refused to surrender the weapons of all able-bodied men? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm stating there that I was told this. I don't know the date. And I believe that the people on the buses were wounded. To what extent, that I don't know. Nor do I know -- sorry, I backtrack. I don't -- you're referring to an agreement which I have already told you I don't believe was an agreement between the military and yourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now take a look at D173. That's the statement of Mr. Edward Joseph. He testified in these proceedings. He speaks about this situation because he was there in the field, and it was an agreement between me and those people, not between Mladic and those people. Can we have paragraph number 20 in D173. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: So let us take a look first at paragraph 19 and then paragraph 20 so that you could understand what Mr. Joseph is referring to. He says: "The previously-mentioned group of slightly wounded men boarded probably the last bus. I recall them being a group of 12. As they were of military age and therefore falling to the problematic group of evacuates, I and Viktor went to VRS General Tolimir who was in the centre area. I asked him if he allows these 12 to go to the Serb-controlled territory without being disturbed and he very clearly replied yes." And now we come to paragraph 20: "The bus departed with the wounded men. And because I still was concerned of their safety, I asked one French officer, probably he was major, to follow the bus with his APC, which he did. Later I heard from the source which I cannot identify that the bus had been stopped and the wounded arrested." So this is what Edward Joseph says. And he was sent to Srebrenica in order to carry out the evacuation of the civilian population. He clearly states that it was on the last day and that this was the last bus. It means that it was after the 27th. This morning we saw the agreement in which the War Presidency signed that all the combatants would surrender their weapons, while they refused to do that, and then send the message to the president of the War Presidency that they would not surrender it. So is this the situation that you mentioned earlier in which you knew that a certain door would be open and by that I mean the door that would enable them to cross the Drina River and go into Serbia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was concentrating on buses and people on it. How have we got to the Drina River? Just let me read what you've said again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Let me help you. Were these able-bodied men stopped on the last day of the evacuation after it was found out that the soldiers did not want to obey the decision for the -- from the War Presidency which bound them to surrender their weapons? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think they are able-bodied. I believe them to be wounded. And I think that's what the -- Joseph says. And that he was still concerned for their safety. The connection between this and my understanding of what was going on with the negotiations over getting people over the Drina, I couldn't put those two together in time as you are describing it. I don't remember the dates well enough to say that this is coincident with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to remind you again of the contents of paragraph 19 of this statement where we find the words: "The previously-mentioned group of slightly wounded men boarded probably the last bus. I recall them being a group of 12. As they were at military age, it meant that they were problematic for the evacuation." So doesn't this say that Mr. Joseph himself identified them as able-bodied men? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say anything of the sort. It says they are a group of wounded men, albeit slightly, and they are of military age.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. So does that mean that their age would define them as men fit for military service or not?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their age would define them as possible for military service. But if they're wounded, then they are hors de combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we find in the English text paragraph 19 the words of Mr. Edward Joseph saying that they were able-bodied, which meant that they were problematic vis-à-vis the evacuation? Thank you. It's the second line in paragraph 19. You can see the words at the very end of the second line that they were able-bodied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, we see another word. "As they were at military age." I don't find the words "able-bodied." Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't know whether this is a perhaps translation issue from the written to the written. I don't see any effort by the Defence to suggest that, so I don't know. That's the only possible explanation other than General Tolimir being obtuse at the moment. But I don't know. But I'm not seeing any suggestion at this point from the Defence that there is a possible translation issue, so we might be able to save some time, otherwise we're just going to go around in circles because we can see what we see in English and we hear the questions coming from General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. Are you able to clarify that, Mr. Tolimir? In the English you see the word "military age."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. If that's what it says in English, it says "military," which means fit for the military. Maybe I could help in order to resolve any misunderstanding. Take a look at D173 which used to be 65 ter 0273. It's a Prosecution document. And that's the document that was introduced by the Prosecution and the Defence received with this translation. And now we can see the translation on the left side of the screen and you can compare it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, this is not the issue we are dealing with. We know that this is the document on the screen. Could you please, to clarify this, read the last sentence of -- the second sentence of paragraph 19 into the record and we will see in which way our interpreters present in the courtroom will translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If I may, it may be easier just to have the interpreters in the booth read what they can see on the screen. Because what's in the writing is in the writing. And we clearly aren't getting anywhere by asking General Tolimir to interpret what he's got or to state the question because we're getting what we're getting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to ask Mr. Tolimir to read the second sentence of paragraph 19. We will be able to follow that. No, third -- it is the third sentence, sorry. Please, Mr. Tolimir, to clarify this, read the third sentence which begins with the words "kako su bili."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm reading from the Serbian version: "As they were able-bodied, which meant that they were problematic about the evacuation, Viktor and I went to see General Tolimir who was in the" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please stop there. It is enough. We wanted to have the -- only the third sentence. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with your permission, maybe I could explain. The phrase in the English language, "military age," is very often translated into Serbian as able-bodied. In practice they are often used as synonyms, to be fit for the military service and to be of the age for the military service. In the Serbian language, you would very rarely say of the military age. So this seems to be only a translation issue, because we are dealing with two terms that are very, very similar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think we all can agree that the English version is the original because Mr. Joseph was interviewed by the OTP in English. Thank you. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, please don't. Please don't carry on because we need now to have our second break. I just realised. We will have our second break and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tolimir, now you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While we still have this statement on the screen, let's look at paragraph 4 and paragraph 5 of the statement. Thank you. It is Mr. Joseph's statement, paragraph 4 and paragraph 5. I quote: "I arrived in Sarajevo and I was briefed there by David Harland, senior civil affairs officer in Sarajevo, and General Rupert Smith, the military commander of UNPROFOR in BiH. I got an impression that the Bosnian Serb forces had attacked and practically overrun Zepa enclave and there was no resistance by the Muslim army in the enclave any more." My question is this: Did you talk to Mr. Joseph before he was sent to Zepa by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the specific incident, but this makes it appear that I did. So I imagine I did. And under the circumstances, I expect I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In that case, I'll move on to paragraph 5: "We decided to go to Zepa, monitor the situation, and probably do as much as possible to help with the evacuation of the civilian population from the enclave. Along with the civil affairs officer Viktor Bezruchenko, I was chosen to do this. I don't remember whether one of us was ordered to be in charge." I want to look at the first sentence of paragraph 7 next. "I believe we departed from Sarajevo on the 19th of July." This is just to give you the temporal context. My question is this: Did you decide for the two officers, Viktor Bezruchenko and Edward Joseph, to be sent there because of the evacuation of the civilian population from Zepa to BiH territory?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I think I've said already, I don't recall making the specific decision. I certainly was content and pleased that they were there. And the first priority and why I wanted people there was to ensure that incidents such as those that was becoming clear might have occurred in Srebrenica weren't going to occur in Zepa, and I wanted to get UN personnel on the ground in the vicinity, observing what was going on as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll now look at paragraphs 16 and 17, where Mr. Joseph confirmed it. Let's go to paragraphs 16 and 17, please. There he says as follows. I quote from Edward Joseph's statement, which is D173, paragraph 16.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please wait a moment until the relevant part is occurring on the screen. Now it is visible. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm quoting from paragraph 16: "We created written lists of the evacuees. And as far as I can recall we had a separate list for each vehicle. I handed over those lists later either to the UNHCR or someone in UNPROFOR. We also tried to place one UNPROFOR soldier in each vehicle, but I'm not sure if we managed to do so throughout the duration of the evacuation." Paragraph 17 -- let me ask you this first: Having read paragraph 16, tell us whether Mr. Joseph reported correctly his role as UNPROFOR representative in the evacuation of the civilians from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is as much as I remember it. And I remember wanting him to record the names of all the people that went on the buses so that we had some idea of who they were, and if any went missing we could account for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 17, he says: "The evacuation probably lasted a bit over three days. The atmosphere was tense throughout the time, but we managed to get all those people on board who had come to the centre of town and were willing to go. I estimate that approximately 7.000 people were evacuated." My question is this: Does Viktor Bezruchenko state here that he evacuated all those who had come to the centre of the town and were willing to leave? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he doesn't. I think it's Ed Joseph's report, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Apologies, it's Mr. Joseph. Did he state there that he managed to board all those who had come to the town centre?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the paragraph states that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us look at how the evacuation process developed as was recorded by the cameramen you requested to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P740. The time is 36 minutes, 14 seconds to 37 minutes, 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, please stop. It was stopped at 36 minutes, 39 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: While watching the video, did you see any VRS members in front of the bus or could you only see civilians boarding the buses in the centre of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any military at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go on with the footage starting with 36 minutes, 39 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Your microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The time is now 36 seconds [as interpreted], 47 seconds. In the previous still we saw some VRS soldiers standing on the side away from the bus. We can also see an ABiH soldier approaching his family. And we see another one greeting his family. Were they prevented from doing so by the VRS? Were they prevented from doing anything in the area?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: This you would -- I'm not clear that those are Bosnian military. I've seen a picture that I recognise as Bosnian Serb. I don't recognise this on the frame I've got in front of me as a -- as Bosnian military.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To have a continuity, could we please go back from the still where we saw the VRS soldiers so that the witness could try and identify any differences in uniform or insignia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you stop it there, that I recognise, particularly the armed person on the left of the group of three, as Bosnian Serb. And if we were to come in closer or it moves, I don't know, there's some insignia on him. On his arm or jacket. No, I can't see very clearly, no. But I certainly see that as a Bosnian Serb soldier. You got someone in a UN hat back left who I don't recognise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please indicate which makes you certain that this is a Bosnian Serb soldier?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- what makes it certain, the camouflage uniform. The colour of the camouflage uniform and the nature of the uniform was frequently worn by the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about the men, the two men on the right side of the picture?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't see this -- the particular soldier with the black hat or scarf around his head, I'm -- thought I'd seen an insignia on his arm. I don't mean that necessarily as a badge. The Bosnian Serb army is -- particularly, if they were doing an attack, would put coloured ribbons on their shoulders to identify them in that attack, so it was quite clear. And this colour coding, if you like, would be specific for that attack. And then they knew that this chap was or someone else was impersonating them or something like that. And I thought I'd seen that on that particular soldier when the first time it had gone through. The other soldiers appear to be from a different unit by the nature of their uniforms, but I wouldn't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Smith. We see three soldiers in this still. You identified them as VRS. And we also see three ABiH soldiers who are partially dressed in uniform and partially in civil clothes greeting their families to the left of these three. Are these three paying any attention to the other three? Are they doing anything with regard to that group? That's one thing. The second thing, on the upper right arm of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please, please, not a compound question, please. It's very difficult to follow. Not a compound. You put one question to the witness including a statement how you identify the three people on the left side of the screen. We want to hear the witness and his opinion about these.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, I want to hear the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the witness would like to see the picture you're referring to. Because I can't see three people to the left of the ... on the screen that I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We all have the same picture on the screen at the moment. I understand, Mr. Tolimir, that he was referring to the people left to this specific soldier you testified about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think those are -- I see no reason to suppose that those are Bosnian military.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now your second question, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see three men to the left of the VRS soldier, the closest to us? Can you see three men wearing items of clothing which is uniform and civilian clothes? It's a combination. One, for example, has civilian pants and a civilian jacket, the other way, the other way around. One of them, for example, has an olive drab uniform. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see four people to the left of the VRS soldier. And to be sure we're looking at the same one, one of the four has what to me on this screen looks like a blue basketball cap on his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us start playing again and then we can see any further differences between VRS soldiers and soldiers from Zepa and representatives of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We started at 36 minutes 44 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is 37 minutes, 3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see the back of a person. Did you personally know Avdo Palic?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know Palic personally.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask to go on playing this footage from 37 minutes, 3 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Did you see the person who is now with his back turned to us in the light blue shirt? Did you notice him holding sheets of paper or lists in his hand?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw a piece of paper in his hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We stopped at 37 minutes, 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us go on with the footage from 37 minutes, 15 seconds. We can probably see the person's face somewhat later, and then stop when we do, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We did already.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The footage is stopped at 37 minutes, 31 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see what the cameraman inserted in the footage by way of titles which probably refer to the person who is now facing us whom you saw a moment ago holding pieces of paper?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you ever met this person? As we can see from the footage, his name is Mehmed Hajric. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall meeting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he introduced to you as the president of the Zepa War Presidency who signed the agreement on the disarmament of men fit for military service?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I don't recall meeting him.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's go on with the footage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Do you recognise anyone in this still?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- well, if we can step it back a bit, I think we have General Mladic on my left but I'm not sure. It's not that clear. We've already identified or you identified the man Palic to the right. And the man with the beard is the man who I'd met at the top of the hill and is the doctor. I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We stopped at 37 minutes, 45 seconds. The witness requested to move a bit back so that we can see the man on the left more clearly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not sure it is Mladic now. Not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Please move a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you see any VRS representatives here greeting Avdo Palic in the presence of Benjamin Kulovac whom you met previously and you recognised him just now?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the man on the left who I thought was Mladic and I don't think it is now is from wearing the uniform of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We stopped now at 37 minutes, 47 seconds. We should move a bit further.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Does the person in the VRS uniform resemble at all General Tolimir perhaps?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as I remember him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let us move on from 37 minutes, 49 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This was the last still of that part of the footage, where you saw the evacuation from Zepa itself. We unfortunately don't have enough time to view everything.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us have a look at P736 briefly so that the witness could see the first and last name of the president of the War Presidency in Zepa. Thank you. In the English could we see the signature block. It was a decision of the Zepa War Presidency. We'd like to have it in English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We can see the names here. The first person is Mehmed Hajric; the second, Hamdija Torlak; the third, Amir Imamovic. As members of the Zepa War Presidency. Did you see the superscript on the footage with Mehmed Hajric's name who appears here as a member of the Zepa War Presidency? Did you see his name on the footage a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see him taking part in the creation of the lists and the evacuation itself?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him holding the lists and seeing people onto the buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I promised you that we would show you how the evacuation started because you asked for that previously.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it now please be displayed. D55, page 29, paragraph 105. Thank you. [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Bezruchenko's report. This is a document that he wrote as a Prosecution expert. Thank you. So could we have paragraph 105.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I'm going to quote it: "UNPROFOR started evacuation from Zepa on the 25th of July. In the afternoon of the 25th of July, French Battalion 2 of Sector Sarajevo sent a medevac convoy to Zepa for evacuation of the wounded." And now my question: Did UNPROFOR take part in this, in the evacuation of the wounded from Zepa? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at line 6 of paragraph 105. This is what it says: "Another convoy reached Zepa at 2300 hours on the 25th of July but did not participate in the evacuation of civilians. The second convoy for the same purpose was blocked near Sarajevo at the first VRS check-point after the airport between 500 hours to 1200 hours and then left for Zepa without an Egyptian APC as was demanded by the VRS." Now, this is my question: Had another special unit of UNPROFOR arrived in Zepa in order to provide security to the evacuation effort? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. On the hill of Boksanica, is that where that special unit was stationed, where the negotiations between the two sides on the separation line took place?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember a special unit. I remember bringing in extra forces which were provided by the French. The exact number, again, I can't recall. If that's what you're referring to, again I don't remember the dates on which they deployed. We've already seen evidence of them being withdrawn in early August.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please say whether the Army of Republika Srpska asked you not to send APCs to Sanicari [as interpreted] in Republika Srpska in order for the asphalt not to be damaged because we could not repair it during the war. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's not --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Sanicari" was not recorded. But I can show, if necessary, a document in which the Main Staff is asking UNPROFOR not to send such vehicles. We can deal with that perhaps if we have time tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Please tell us whether this French unit that arrived at Boksanica was part of the rapid deployment force. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't. It came from Sector Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember who the commander of this unit was and what his name was? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall, no. No, I don't. No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at paragraph 106 of this document. Thank you. It reads as follows: "UNPROFOR Sector Sarajevo report for the 26th of July described the situation as follows: "In accordance with the order of UNPROFOR commander and decision of sector commander, our units took part in the evacuation of wounded people from Zepa to Sarajevo and civilian population to Kladanj. This process is on-going." 161 is the document that was quoted by Prosecution expert Mr. Bezruchenko and you can see that, 161, and you can see its ERN number down there in the footnote. Thank you. Now, did UNPROFOR, as is stated here, take part in the evacuation of the wounded and the civilian population? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, I think it was the fourth or fifth time that you asked this question. You should avoid pure repetitions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not going repeat that question any more because the witness gave a clear answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please look at the third sentence in paragraph 106, the last line: "General Tolimir respected the evacuation agreement and that BSA apparently was seeking to complete the evacuation on the 26th of July." And there is a document about that in footnote 162. This is information provided by G2 SHQ on the 26th of July, 1995. Thank you. Can you see this and can you confirm that such reports arrived in Sector Sarajevo and the command of UNPROFOR in Sarajevo? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can see what's written in that paragraph and that their reference to Sector Sarajevo reports, which as I've said before, is a subordinate command to mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have paragraph 109 of this report of Mr. Bezruchenko, who was an expert of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: This is what he says in paragraph 109: "On the 26th of July, 1995, President Izetbegovic sent a message to Palic, demanding to put under control those soldiers who were going to surrender. The message also contained a vague promise to arrange an exchange." And now we're going to read the content of the message: "There is information that a certain number of your soldiers is moving towards the village with the intention of surrendering. I do not know if this is correct. Warn them about the danger and put them under control. Negotiations about exchange are in progress. We have enough arguments to obtain good conditions of exchange because we keep a great number of their prisoners, but we have to be careful what we are doing. And something else, important, burn all archives and letters." End of quotation. Greeting, Alija Izetbegovic, Sarajevo, the 26th of July, 1995. This telegram was sent from Sarajevo to Zepa at 16.45 and that is what is referred to in footnote 165. And also the ERN number of the document on the basis of which the expert came to this conclusion is noted. Please tell us whether Alija Izetbegovic was stopping soldiers from acting in accordance with the provisions of the agreement and reaching the UNPROFOR base in Zepa and handing over their weapons?

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we still referring to the document that you showed me this morning as the agreement?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm referring to the agreement on disarming, the one I showed you this morning several times. And now we are reading what Alija Izetbegovic says about that agreement. So could we please hear now whether it is clear on this basis that he was stopping some of the soldiers from reaching the centre and acting in accordance with the agreement as was stated in paragraph 6 [as interpreted] of that decision you saw a moment ago? Yes, the decision of the War Presidency, that all military-aged men surrender their weapons. D51, I can show that again, and P736, and that is a reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This again is the problem, Mr. Tolimir. We have discussed and seen at least three so-called agreements. Now you are referring to the decision of the War Presidency of the 27th of July, 1995. This is P736 and not D51. You should be clear in your questioning, and the witness asked for that, to make clear to which of these three different agreements you are referring. I take it now that you were referring to the decision of the War Presidency of the 27th of July, 1995, which is not an agreement about demilitarisation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said D51. That is the agreement that the witness saw this morning. And in addition to the agreement, it is regulated by the decision that you refer to a moment ago, so I don't have to repeat that. These two documents regulate what the soldiers are going to do. I now read what Alija Izetbegovic wrote. Did he stop the soldiers from reaching the centre of Zepa and disarming in accordance with the provisions of the agreement and decision on disarmament. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Tolimir, this is not clear, at least to me. You put first the question, please tell us whether Alija Izetbegovic was stopping soldiers from acting in accordance with the provisions of the agreement. We have dealt with three agreements and you, now again, at least you were referring to two agreements. You should be very clear in your questioning. Which agreement do you mean now? D51 or P736? And if you do that, please put it on the screen. Otherwise, it will help nobody in understanding the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness please remember what Alija wrote to Palic in paragraph 109 and then can we have D51 placed on the screen. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: We see this now, that this is the agreement of the 24th of July. Thank you. And we also see paragraph 2 that we read out this morning: "Avdo Palic shall issue an order to his troops to withdraw from the defence line and refugee groups together with the population and from the centre of settlements/villages, and not to try to cross illegally through the territory of Republika Srpska." Thank you. In that telegram of the 26th that we saw, did Alija Izetbegovic stop the process of surrender of the military-aged men? And it says here, "moving towards the village." And it says, "I don't know how that is developing and place them under control." Is he actually stopping the soldiers from acting in accordance with the agreement reached on the 24th between the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RUPERT ANTHONY SMITH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he is saying to Palic is that he want to be -- he wants him, Palic, to get all of his command under control. And the reason for that is because he's heard that some of them are intending to surrender. And warn them of the dangers of doing so. And then goes on to tell Palic that negotiations are underway. The -- the tone of this is that he, President Izetbegovic, and Palic, are setting out to do something that does not involve surrendering. I hear that other people in your command, is what he's saying, are setting out to surrender. I'm not convinced from this that Izetbegovic knows of this agreement of the 24th of July. He might have done, but I'm not convinced from the tone of his message that he knows that Palic has signed up to everybody surrendering at paragraph 2 of that agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Smith, please, let us have a look at paragraph 85 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, you should look at the time. You are already five minutes past our time-frame. We can't go on and on. We should adjourn for the day at a certain point in time. As always, I don't want to interrupt you, but you yourself are responsible for recognising the time. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't want to extend it any second longer than we have to, but we had an 11-hour time estimate which we've got no problem with. We obviously lost some time with technical difficulties, I went over about half an hour. We thought we were going to be able to conclude General Smith's testimony in the four days. I sincerely doubt we'll be able to if the Defence takes its full 11 hours. So I don't know the General's schedule, but for our witness planning purposes as well, it's helpful for us to know where we're headed, schedule-wise, into next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: To let the parties know, Mr. Tolimir has now used 6 hours and 10 minutes for his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, can you give us an estimation of the remainder of your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I think that we will be done with the cross-examination by the 11 hours that we had announced. We are not going to ask for longer hours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: That makes it clear that we have to continue next week. It is not possible to finish tomorrow. Is that for the moment enough for you, Mr. Thayer, for your planning purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we aren't in a position to speak with General Smith except indirectly through VWU about his schedule and they can take care of that, but I wanted to make sure that we all understood what the future was going to look like, particularly the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you be available next week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible, Mr. President. I would need to make a telephone call later on this afternoon and check my diary, but I think it might be possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We would appreciate that to enable Mr. Tolimir to conclude his examination in the estimated time. Thank you very much for your understanding. We have to adjourn for the day, and we'll resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of March, 2011, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.53 p.m.,
